questions.q: After India’s 16th general election, how does the editorial describe the proper role of the losing party?
options: To withdraw from public life until the next election
Not quite. The article says: A supporting role in national development, not opposition for its own sake.
A supporting role in national development, not opposition for its own sake
Yes. In a democracy both sides are winners.
To block the new government wherever possible
Not quite. The article says: A supporting role in national development, not opposition for its own sake.
To form a rival government
Not quite. The article says: A supporting role in national development, not opposition for its own sake.
questions.rationale: “The role of the opposition is not that of a political rival; rather, it is a role of participation… it is destined to perform a supporting role.”

questions.q: How does the motto of democracy differ from that of kingship, in the editorial’s words?
options: “I am here to serve the land,” not “I am here to rule the land”
Right. Victory is a responsibility, not a cause for pride.
“I am here for life”
Not quite. The article says: “I am here to serve the land,” not “I am here to rule the land”.
“I am here to change the constitution”
Not quite. The article says: “I am here to serve the land,” not “I am here to rule the land”.
“I am here to reward my supporters”
Not quite. The article says: “I am here to serve the land,” not “I am here to rule the land”.
questions.rationale: “In the kingship era, the motto was: ‘I am here to rule the land’, but in a democracy the motto is quite different. It is: ‘I am here to serve the land.’”

questions.q: What link does the article draw between fasting and dua (supplication)?
options: Fasting replaces the need for dua
Not quite. The article says: Fasting builds patience and a humble heart, from which sincere prayer rises.
Fasting builds patience and a humble heart, from which sincere prayer rises
Yes. “Real fasting is that which induces real dua.”
Dua shortens the hours of the fast
Not quite. The article says: Fasting builds patience and a humble heart, from which sincere prayer rises.
Dua is only accepted during the fast
Not quite. The article says: Fasting builds patience and a humble heart, from which sincere prayer rises.
questions.rationale: “Patience is the ground on which the blessed tree of dua is grown… Fasting increases the spiritual capability of a man’s heart.”

questions.q: Why is Ramazan called “the month of sympathy”?
options: Because people greet each other more often
Not quite. The article says: For some hours the well-off share the hunger and thirst the poor know daily.
For some hours the well-off share the hunger and thirst the poor know daily
Correct. Fasting teaches what basic needs are.
Because the sick are excused from fasting
Not quite. The article says: For some hours the well-off share the hunger and thirst the poor know daily.
Because quarrels are forbidden by law
Not quite. The article says: For some hours the well-off share the hunger and thirst the poor know daily.
questions.rationale: “For a few hours, the rich also come to live in the same conditions in which a poor man lives.”

questions.q: A neighbour said he could not accept Islam: the saint’s religion seemed beyond his strength, and the common people’s made him ashamed. What does the article conclude?
options: The neighbour was looking for excuses
Not quite. The article says: Both are distortions; Islam in its original sources is simple, natural and appealing.
Both are distortions; Islam in its original sources is simple, natural and appealing
Well read. Later additions hid its true face.
Islam is meant only for saints
Not quite. The article says: Both are distortions; Islam in its original sources is simple, natural and appealing.
Ordinary believers cannot practise religion
Not quite. The article says: Both are distortions; Islam in its original sources is simple, natural and appealing.
questions.rationale: “Islam is a simple and natural religion… If all the artificial veils are lifted and Islam’s true face is seen, it will be recognized as the voice of human nature.”

questions.q: In what spirit should a person give Zakat, according to the article?
options: As a tax owed to the ruler
Not quite. The article says: As handing others their rightful share of what God has given, without any sense of doing a favour.
As handing others their rightful share of what God has given, without any sense of doing a favour
Yes. All one owns is from God.
As a payment to be returned with interest
Not quite. The article says: As handing others their rightful share of what God has given, without any sense of doing a favour.
As a generous gift for which thanks are due
Not quite. The article says: As handing others their rightful share of what God has given, without any sense of doing a favour.
questions.rationale: “When a man gives alms to others, he should do so with the knowledge that they have a rightful share in his wealth… He is doing no more than giving others their due.”

questions.q: Why should iftar be a simple meal?
options: A lavish spread turns attention to taste and loses the gratitude and reflection the moment should bring
Right. “A lavish iftar kills the true spirit of fasting.”
Simple food is cheaper for the host
Not quite. The article says: A lavish spread turns attention to taste and loses the gratitude and reflection the moment should bring.
Rich food is unhealthy after a fast
Not quite. The article says: A lavish spread turns attention to taste and loses the gratitude and reflection the moment should bring.
The Prophet disliked eating in company
Not quite. The article says: A lavish spread turns attention to taste and loses the gratitude and reflection the moment should bring.
questions.rationale: “Simplicity saves us from distraction and will make us concentrate on the spiritual aspect of fasting.”

questions.q: What danger does the article see in measuring religion by counted rituals?
options: It makes worship too difficult
Not quite. The article says: It breeds complacency – a person feels his duty is done and stops fearing God.
It discourages people from attending the mosque
Not quite. The article says: It breeds complacency – a person feels his duty is done and stops fearing God.
It leads to disputes over numbers
Not quite. The article says: It breeds complacency – a person feels his duty is done and stops fearing God.
It breeds complacency – a person feels his duty is done and stops fearing God
Exactly. The Companions never felt their deeds were enough.
questions.rationale: “Having quantified his deeds, he feels that he has complied with what was expected of him and therefore becomes complacent.”

questions.q: The last night of Ramazan is called the “night of reward.” How does the article say it is best spent?
options: In prayer, looking back over the month, and making fresh resolve
Yes. Not in shopping and entertainment.
In preparing the Eid feast
Not quite. The article says: In prayer, looking back over the month, and making fresh resolve.
In visiting the markets before they close
Not quite. The article says: In prayer, looking back over the month, and making fresh resolve.
In sleep, to be fresh for the morning
Not quite. The article says: In prayer, looking back over the month, and making fresh resolve.
questions.rationale: “The ‘night of reward’ is best utilised in more prayer and supplication, in introspection of the whole month of Ramazan that has just passed and in making fresh resolutions.”

questions.article: The Relationship Between Fasting and Life
questions.q: To what part of a vehicle does the article compare fasting, and why?
options: The wheels – it keeps life moving
Not quite. The article says: The brakes – restraint over desire is what lets the journey be completed safely.
The lamps – it shows the way at night
Not quite. The article says: The brakes – restraint over desire is what lets the journey be completed safely.
The engine – it supplies energy
Not quite. The article says: The brakes – restraint over desire is what lets the journey be completed safely.
The brakes – restraint over desire is what lets the journey be completed safely
Well read. Half of life’s actions consist in abstaining.
questions.rationale: “The position of fasting in human life is akin to the brakes in an engine… so that he may travel successfully on the path of God.”
